content: Chlorhexidine gluconate is an antibacterial agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of gingivitis, periodontitis, and for use in skin cleansing procedures. It is commonly associated with side effects such as staining of teeth and oral surfaces, formation of calculus, and changes in taste perception. For adults, the FDA-approved indication is the treatment of gingivitis, which is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gums upon probing. The recommended dosage is 15 mL of undiluted solution, used as an oral rinse for 30 seconds twice daily, in the morning and evening after brushing teeth. The safety and efficacy of chlorhexidine gluconate in pediatric patients under 18 years of age have not been established. Off-label uses in adults include conditions such as alveolitis of the jaw, burns, nosocomial infections, dental procedures, prosthetic dental implants, oral infections, and sensitive dentin. However, there is limited information regarding off-label use in pediatric patients. Chlorhexidine gluconate should not be used in individuals with known hypersensitivity to the drug or its components. It has not been proven effective for periodontitis, and its use may lead to an increase in supragingival calculus. Subgingival calculus formation has not been studied. Regular dental prophylaxis, at intervals no longer than six months, is recommended to remove calculus deposits. Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Staining of oral surfaces, including teeth, restorations, and the tongue, is a common side effect. Not all patients will experience significant staining, but it is more pronounced in those with heavy plaque accumulation. Stains can generally be removed through professional dental cleaning, though additional time may be required. Patients with anterior facial restorations that are rough or have margins may experience permanent discoloration, and in rare cases, replacement of restorations may be necessary. Some patients may also experience temporary or, in rare cases, permanent alterations in taste perception. The most common adverse reactions observed in clinical trials include increased staining of teeth and oral surfaces, increased calculus formation, and changes in taste perception. Other reported side effects include oral irritation, allergic reactions, and various oral mucosal conditions such as ulcers, erythema, desquamation, and coated tongue. Post-marketing reports have noted symptoms such as stomatitis, gingivitis, glossitis, ulcers, dry mouth, and paresthesia. Rarely, swelling of the parotid gland or inflammation of salivary glands has been reported. Chlorhexidine gluconate is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA, meaning animal studies have not shown harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. It is unknown whether the drug is excreted in human milk, so caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. There is no specific guidance on its use in labor and delivery, pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, racial, renal, hepatic, or immunocompromised populations. Chlorhexidine gluconate oral rinse should be used immediately following a dental prophylaxis. Patients should be reevaluated and receive professional cleaning at intervals no longer than six months. After rinsing, patients should not rinse with water or other mouthwashes, brush their teeth, or eat immediately. The product is not intended for ingestion and should be expectorated after use. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate that approximately 30% of the active ingredient is retained in the oral cavity after rinsing, with slow release into oral fluids. Chlorhexidine gluconate is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with most of the drug excreted in feces and less than 1% excreted in urine. In cases of overdose, ingestion of 1–2 ounces by a small child (~10 kg body weight) may cause gastric distress, including nausea. Medical attention should be sought if more than 4 ounces are ingested by a small child. Chlorhexidine gluconate is supplied as a 0.12% oral rinse in pink liquid form, available in 4 fl oz (118 mL) and 16 fl oz (473 mL) amber plastic bottles with child-resistant caps. It should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with permissible excursions to 15–30°C (59–86°F).
